title: Randomised Algorithms: Las Vegas and Monte Carlo

blocks.text: How can randomness help algorithms run faster or be simpler? Explore the power of randomised algorithms in defeating adversarial inputs.

blocks.markdown: Randomised algorithms use random numbers to influence their behavior. They can offer significant advantages in terms of simplicity and efficiency, especially when dealing with complex or adversarial inputs.

blocks.title: Randomised Algorithms
blocks.text: A randomised algorithm is an algorithm that makes random choices during its process to achieve a result.

blocks.markdown: There are two primary types of randomised algorithms: Las Vegas and Monte Carlo. Understanding the differences between them is crucial for selecting the right approach.

blocks.title: Las Vegas Algorithms
blocks.text: Las Vegas algorithms always produce the correct result, but their running time is a random variable.

blocks.title: Monte Carlo Algorithms
blocks.text: Monte Carlo algorithms have a deterministic running time but may produce incorrect results with a certain probability.

blocks.markdown: Let's consider a classic example of a randomised algorithm: Randomised Quicksort. This algorithm uses randomness to select a pivot, which helps to avoid the worst-case scenarios of the deterministic version.

blocks.title: Expected Running Time of Randomised Quicksort
blocks.prompt: Analyze the expected running time of Randomised Quicksort for an array of size $n$.

steps.text: Randomised Quicksort selects a pivot randomly, partitioning the array into two subarrays.
The expected number of comparisons in Randomised Quicksort is given by the recurrence relation: $T(n) = n + \frac{1}{n} \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} (T(k) + T(n-k-1))$.
Solving this recurrence relation, we find that the expected running time is $O(n \log n)$.

blocks.answer: The expected running time of Randomised Quicksort is $O(n \log n)$.

blocks.markdown: Randomisation helps algorithms avoid worst-case inputs. By making decisions randomly, the algorithm becomes less predictable and harder for an adversary to manipulate.

blocks.title: Randomisation Defeating Adversarial Inputs
blocks.prompt: Explain why randomisation in algorithms can defeat adversarial worst-case inputs.

steps.text: Consider an adversary who knows the deterministic pivot selection of Quicksort.
The adversary can construct an input that forces the worst-case running time of $O(n^2)$.
By selecting the pivot randomly, the adversary cannot predict the pivot, thus making it unlikely to consistently force the worst-case scenario.

blocks.answer: Randomisation prevents adversaries from predicting and exploiting deterministic behavior, thus avoiding worst-case scenarios.

blocks.title: Key Point
blocks.text: Randomised algorithms can offer significant performance improvements by avoiding predictable patterns that adversaries can exploit.

points: Las Vegas algorithms guarantee correct results but have variable running times.
Monte Carlo algorithms have fixed running times but may produce incorrect results with some probability.
Randomisation helps algorithms avoid worst-case inputs and improve average performance.
